steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Studying families: sensitive topics (divorce, domestic violence). Questionnaires miss depth; interviews capture experiences but may distress; observations are intrusive. Official statistics provide marriage/divorce rates.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Studying education: access requires permission (gatekeepers). Questionnaires survey many quickly; interviews explore experiences; observations see classroom dynamics (Hawthorne effect); statistics show exam results; documents include Ofsted reports.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Studying crime: victim surveys capture unreported crime; self-report studies reveal hidden offending; observations study deviant subcultures (ethical issues); statistics are readily available but distorted; field experiments test discrimination.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Choosing methods: practical (time, money, access), ethical (consent, harm), and theoretical considerations (reliability vs validity, positivism vs interpretivism).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: A researcher wants to study the impact of divorce on children. Evaluate which method would be most appropriate. | Compare the practical and ethical issues of researching crime vs education. | Evaluate whether triangulation always produces better research than a single method.

steps.body: Semi-structured interviews: allow children to express experiences, follow up on sensitive topics, build rapport. steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Choose methods based on: PRACTICAL, ETHICAL, THEORETICAL factors. Positivism = quantitative (reliable). Interpretivism = qualitative (meaningful). Both contribute. Triangulation = combine methods. Quantitative shows WHAT, qualitative explains WHY.
